claim: The important contributions of Bdf1/2 to transcription extend beyond TFIID function.

claim: Bdf1/2 co-occupy the majority of yeast promoters.

claim: Hypersensitivity of genes to Bdf1/2 depletion results from combined defects in transcription initiation and early elongation.
source: Surprisingly, we discovered that hypersensitivity of genes to Bdf1/2 depletion results from combined defects in transcription initiation and early elongation, a striking functional similarity to human BET proteins, most notably Brd4.

claim: Bdf1/2 are critical for yeast transcription.
source: Our results establish Bdf1/2 as critical for yeast transcription and provide important mechanistic insights into the function of BET proteins in all eukaryotes.

claim: The study provides important mechanistic insights into the function of BET proteins in all eukaryotes.

Rapid Bdf depletion strongly decreases transcription from the TFIID-dependent genes, and, at many genes, the Bdfs are more important than Tafs for normal levels of transcription.

claim: At many genes, the Bdfs are more important than Tafs for normal levels of transcription.
source: Rapid Bdf depletion strongly decreases transcription from the TFIID-dependent genes, and, at many genes, the Bdfs are more important than Tafs for normal levels of transcription.

claim: Bdf1 was efficiently degraded with <10% of protein remaining after 30 min treatment with IAA.

claim: Bdf2 degradation was less complete, with ~15% of protein remaining after 30 min treatment with IAA.

evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Growth of all strains with Bdf derivatives was similar to wild type.
source: Growth of all strains with Bdf derivatives was similar to wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and analysis of 4-thioU mRNA levels in control dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated cultures showed that changes in transcription due to these genetic alterations were minimal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Changes in transcription due to genetic alterations in Bdf strains were minimal in control DMSO-treated cultures.
source: Growth of all strains with Bdf derivatives was similar to wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and analysis of 4-thioU mRNA levels in control dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated cultures showed that changes in transcription due to these genetic alterations were minimal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The variation in nascent mRNA levels between replicate samples was <30% for nearly all experiments.
source: Experiments were done in two or three biological replicates, and the variation in nascent mRNA levels between replicate samples was <30% for nearly all experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by coefficient of variation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Bdf2 degradation or bdf2 deletion showed minimal changes in transcription.
source: Bdf2 degradation or bdf2 deletion showed minimal changes in transcription while Bdf1 degradation resulted in modest defects, in agreement with the genetic phenotypes of BDF1/2 mutants (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and Supplementary file 1).

claim: Bdf1 degradation resulted in modest transcription defects.
source: Bdf2 degradation or bdf2 deletion showed minimal changes in transcription while Bdf1 degradation resulted in modest defects, in agreement with the genetic phenotypes of BDF1/2 mutants (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Depletion of both Bdf1 and Bdf2 resulted in a global collapse of transcription with median decreases of ~4-fold and ~5.4-fold for double degron and Bdf1 degron/bdf2 deletion, respectively.
source: Strikingly, depletion of both Bdf1 and Bdf2, either through a double degron or by combining a bdf2 deletion with a Bdf1 degron, resulted in a global collapse of transcription with median decreases of ~4-fold and ~5.4-fold, respectively (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Transcriptional changes in both Bdf1/2 depletion experiments are highly correlated (r = 0.95).
source: Transcriptional changes in both Bdf1/2 depletion experiments are highly correlated (r = 0.95) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The results of the Bdf1 and Bdf1/2 depletion experiments correlate (r = 0.82), showing redundant roles of Bdf1 and Bdf2 in transcription.
source: The results of the Bdf1 and Bdf1/2 depletion experiments also correlate (r = 0.82), showing redundant roles of Bdf1 and Bdf2 in transcription (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Transcription changes upon Bdf or Taf1 depletion correlate but the relationship between them is not linear.
source: We compared results of the Bdf depletion experiment with previously published results of rapid Taf1 depletion (Donczew et al., 2020). Surprisingly, we observed that transcription changes upon Bdf or Taf1 depletion correlate but the relationship between them is not linear (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Genes less sensitive to Bdf depletion include almost all CR genes and one-third of TFIID-dependent genes.
source: Labeling the points based on the TFIID and CR gene categories revealed that genes less sensitive to Bdf depletion (on the right of the diagonal line) include almost all CR genes and one-third of TFIID-dependent genes.
evidence: This is supported by the scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most of the TFIID-dependent genes (68%) are more sensitive to Bdf than Taf1 depletion.
source: Interestingly, most of the TFIID-dependent genes (68%) are more sensitive to Bdf than Taf1 depletion and, for 12% of them, the difference is fourfold or higher (Supplementary file 1).

claim: For 12% of TFIID-dependent genes, the difference in sensitivity to Bdf versus Taf1 depletion is fourfold or higher.
source: Interestingly, most of the TFIID-dependent genes (68%) are more sensitive to Bdf than Taf1 depletion and, for 12% of them, the difference is fourfold or higher (Supplementary file 1).

claim: Bdf1 and Taf1 are degraded with similar efficiency.

claim: Bdfs have important TFIID-independent contributions to transcription of many genes.

claim: Comparison of the Bdf results with depletion of Taf13 leads to similar conclusions as comparison with Taf1 depletion.

claim: About 95% of RP genes belong to the TFIID-dependent class.

evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

evidence: This is supported by comparative RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 19% of TFIID-dependent genes are similarly sensitive to Ssl2 depletion as they are to Bdf depletion.
source: Interestingly, 38 and 19% of TFIID-dependent genes are similarly sensitive to Toa1 or Ssl2 depletion as they are to Bdf depletion.
evidence: This is supported by comparative RNA-seq data analysis.

evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis of gene sensitivities.

evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Bdf1 is a subunit of the SWR1 complex that incorporates the histone variant H2A.Z into promoter-proximal nucleosomes.

claim: Rapid depletion of H2A.Z did not reveal significant defects in gene transcription.
source: RNA-seq analysis did not reveal significant defects in gene transcription following the rapid loss of H2A.Z (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that the global transcriptional defects upon Bdf depletion are not mediated via SWR1 and H2A.Z.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The global transcriptional defects upon Bdf depletion are not mediated via SWR1 and H2A.Z.
source: RNA-seq analysis did not reveal significant defects in gene transcription following the rapid loss of H2A.Z (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that the global transcriptional defects upon Bdf depletion are not mediated via SWR1 and H2A.Z.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transcriptional defects upon H2A.Z depletion.

claim: Bdf1 was initially proposed to constitute a missing part of yeast Taf1.
source: Bdf1 was initially proposed to constitute a missing part of yeast Taf1 (Matangkasombut et al., 2000), but later work classified Bdf1/2 as members of the BET family based on a conserved domain organization (Wu and Chiang, 2007; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Later work classified Bdf1/2 as members of the BET family based on a conserved domain organization.
source: Bdf1 was initially proposed to constitute a missing part of yeast Taf1 (Matangkasombut et al., 2000), but later work classified Bdf1/2 as members of the BET family based on a conserved domain organization (Wu and Chiang, 2007; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Bdf1 BDs, especially BD2, are more closely related to Brd4 than hTaf1 BDs.
source: Multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis of individual BDs of Bdf1, Brd4, and human Taf1 (hTaf1) revealed that Bdf1 BDs, especially BD2, are more closely related to Brd4 than hTaf1 BDs (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Other conserved domains of Bdf1 and Brd4 show ≥50% similarity.
source: Other conserved domains of Bdf1 and Brd4 show ≥50% similarity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TATA-less genes in both yeast and human systems were significantly more affected by Bdf/BET depletion than TATA-containing genes.
source: We found that TATA-less genes in both systems were significantly more affected by Bdf/BET depletion than TATA-containing genes (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In the 25% most affected genes in yeast and human datasets, there is an extensive overlap in major gene ontology terms.
source: Finally, in the 25% most affected genes in each dataset, we observed an extensive overlap in major gene ontology terms (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Bdf1 and Bdf2 have similar genome-wide binding patterns with broad peak spanning between −1 and +1 nucleosomes and signals extending into the gene body.
source: Comparison of Bdf1/2 and Taf1 ChEC-seq showed similar binding patterns with broad peak spanning between −1 and +1 nucleosomes and signals extending into the gene body, especially for Bdf1 (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 3700 promoters are bound by Bdf1.
source: We identified 3700, 3466, and 3103 promoters bound by Bdf1, Bdf2, and Taf1, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq peak calling analysis.

claim: 3466 promoters are bound by Bdf2.
source: We identified 3700, 3466, and 3103 promoters bound by Bdf1, Bdf2, and Taf1, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq peak calling analysis.

claim: 3103 promoters are bound by Taf1.
source: We identified 3700, 3466, and 3103 promoters bound by Bdf1, Bdf2, and Taf1, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq peak calling analysis.

claim: There is an extensive overlap of promoters bound by both Bdfs and the signals at common bound promoters are highly correlated.
source: There is an extensive overlap of promoters bound by both Bdfs and the signals at common bound promoters are highly correlated, although Bdf1 signals are consistently stronger, in agreement with its dominant role (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bdf1 signals are consistently stronger than Bdf2 signals, in agreement with its dominant role.
source: There is an extensive overlap of promoters bound by both Bdfs and the signals at common bound promoters are highly correlated, although Bdf1 signals are consistently stronger, in agreement with its dominant role (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is extensive overlap between Bdf1 and Taf1 bound promoters.
source: There is also extensive overlap between Bdf1 and Taf1 bound promoters (Figure 2B), although Bdf1 is found less frequently at CR genes (Figure 2C), consistent with the lesser role of Bdfs at this gene class.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Bdf1 is found less frequently at CR genes, consistent with the lesser role of Bdfs at this gene class.
source: There is also extensive overlap between Bdf1 and Taf1 bound promoters (Figure 2B), although Bdf1 is found less frequently at CR genes (Figure 2C), consistent with the lesser role of Bdfs at this gene class.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Bdf1 chromatin occupancy is only weakly predictive of the gene dependence on Bdf1/2.
source: Interestingly, the Bdf1 chromatin occupancy is only weakly predictive of the gene dependence on Bdf1/2, as was similarly reported for human BET factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Muhar et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citations to prior literature.

claim: Bdf1 ChIP-seq results are similar to ChEC-seq as well as to previously published ChIP-exo data.
source: We validated Bdf1 binding using ChIP-seq as an orthogonal approach. The results are similar to ChEC-seq as well as to previously published ChIP-exo data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 3; Rhee and Pugh, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citation to prior literature.

claim: The number of bound promoters detected by ChIP-seq is lower than ChEC-seq due to worse signal to background ratio.
source: The number of bound promoters detected by ChIP-seq is lower due to worse signal to background ratio but shows a good overlap with ChEC-seq results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Bdf2 ChIP-seq signals correlate well with Bdf1 ChIP-seq signals at promoters bound by Bdf1.
source: We also performed a Bdf2 ChIP-seq experiment, but the quality of the data was too low to call peaks. Instead, we calculated Bdf2 signal at promoters bound by Bdf1 and found that the signals correlate well, supporting conclusions obtained by ChEC-seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, F and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, F.

claim: 15% of RP promoters have detectable Bdf1 binding by ChEC-seq.
source: However, a major difference between ChEC-seq and ChIP-seq was observed at the RP genes. We detected Bdf1 binding at 15% of RP promoters using ChEC-seq, which is consistent with a limited role of Bdfs at RP genes.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 94% of RP promoters have a significant Bdf1 ChIP signal.
source: Conversely, almost all (94%) RP promoters have a significant Bdf1 ChIP signal, but this result is not predictive of Bdf1 function (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: For both TFIID-dependent and CR gene classes, the normalized H4K12ac level at promoters significantly differs depending on the presence of a Bdf1 peak.
source: Importantly, for both classes of genes, the normalized H4K12ac level at promoters significantly differs depending on the presence of a Bdf1 peak (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At many promoters Bdf1 occupancy predicts higher H4K12ac levels and transcription dependence on Bdfs.
source: To conclude, at many promoters Bdf1 occupancy predicts higher H4K12ac levels and transcription dependence on Bdfs.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Bdf1 binding and H4K12ac levels.

claim: Following Bdf1 depletion, the Bdf2 signal increases at TFIID promoters at the expense of CR promoters.
source: Following Bdf1 depletion, the Bdf2 signal increases at TFIID promoters at the expense of CR promoters (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Changes in Bdf2 occupancy at individual promoters after Bdf1 depletion are relatively weak but correlate well with gene dependence on Bdfs (r = −0.52).
source: The changes at individual promoters are relatively weak but they correlate well with gene dependence on Bdfs (r = −0.52) (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Bdf1 does not redistribute in response to Bdf2 depletion.
source: Conversely, Bdf1 does not redistribute in response to Bdf2 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Bdf2 redistribution after Bdf1 depletion provides evidence of redundancy between Bdf1 and Bdf2, with Bdf1 being the dominant factor and Bdf2 serving an auxiliary role.
source: This result provides more evidence of redundancy between Bdf1 and Bdf2, with Bdf1 being the dominant factor and Bdf2 serving an auxiliary role.
evidence: This is inferred from the redistribution pattern of Bdf2 upon Bdf1 depletion.

claim: Esa1 is almost exclusively responsible for acetylation of lysines 5, 8, and 12 on histone H4 in yeast.
source: Esa1, a catalytic subunit of the NuA4 complex, is almost exclusively responsible for acetylation of lysines 5, 8, and 12 on histone H4 in yeast (Chang and Pillus, 2009; Suka et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 1 hr treatment with IAA allowed for a substantial loss of both H4K12ac and Esa1.
source: We used a 1 hr treatment with IAA, which allowed for a substantial loss of both H4K12ac and Esa1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 4-thioU RNA-seq analysis revealed a global loss of transcription after Esa1 depletion, which has a good but nonlinear correlation with the Bdf experiment (r = 0.73).
source: 4-thioU RNA-seq analysis revealed a global loss of transcription after Esa1 depletion, which has a good but nonlinear correlation with the Bdf experiment (r = 0.73) (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Bdf depletion results in stronger transcriptional defects than Esa1 depletion, suggesting that a portion of Bdf function is H4Ac independent.
source: Importantly, Bdf depletion results in stronger transcriptional defects, suggesting that a portion of Bdf function is H4Ac independent.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis of transcriptional defects.

claim: Bdf1/2, Esa1, and TFIID cooperate in regulation of many genes, but their contributions to transcription can be significantly different at individual genes.
source: Our findings show that Bdf1/2, Esa1, and TFIID cooperate in regulation of many genes, but their contributions to transcription can be significantly different at individual genes (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: After 1 hr of IAA treatment, the H4K12ac chromatin signal decreased dramatically, but Bdf1 was still bound at substantial levels, especially at promoters.
source: After 1 hr of IAA treatment, the H4K12ac chromatin signal decreased dramatically, but Bdf1 was still bound at substantial levels, especially at promoters (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and ChEC-seq data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The quantified changes in Bdf1 promoter signal and transcription following Esa1 depletion are correlated, suggesting that the effect of Esa1 on transcription is largely mediated by Bdf1.
source: Nevertheless, the quantified changes in Bdf1 promoter signal and transcription following Esa1 depletion are correlated, suggesting that the effect of Esa1 on transcription is largely mediated by Bdf1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Brd4 was detected at human promoters following BD inhibition or mutation.
source: Consistent with our results, Brd4 was also detected at human promoters following BD inhibition or mutation, which explains why BET degradation outperforms BET inhibition in preclinical cancer models (Bauer et al., 2021; Kanno et al., 2014; Winter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BET degradation outperforms BET inhibition in preclinical cancer models.
source: Consistent with our results, Brd4 was also detected at human promoters following BD inhibition or mutation, which explains why BET degradation outperforms BET inhibition in preclinical cancer models (Bauer et al., 2021; Kanno et al., 2014; Winter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The residual binding of Bdfs in the absence of H4 acetylation may be due to interactions with other histone acetylation marks.
source: It is possible that the residual binding of Bdfs in the absence of H4 acetylation is due to interactions with other histone acetylation marks. For example, Bdf1 was shown to have weak affinity for acetylated histone H3 (Matangkasombut and Buratowski, 2003).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Bdf1 was shown to have weak affinity for acetylated histone H3.
source: For example, Bdf1 was shown to have weak affinity for acetylated histone H3 (Matangkasombut and Buratowski, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BET recruitment can be mediated by interactions with transcription factors (TFs), coactivators, or chromatin remodelers.
source: It has also been proposed that BET recruitment can be mediated by interactions with transcription factors (TFs), coactivators, or chromatin remodelers, and it will be interesting to investigate if such mechanisms play a role in Bdf targeting (Lambert et al., 2019; Rahman et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human BET factors are involved in recruitment of Mediator.
source: Human BET factors are involved in recruitment of Mediator (Bhagwat et al., 2016), and Bdf1/2 were proposed to assist in recruitment of TFIID to yeast promoters (Matangkasombut et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Modest (~1.7-fold) decreases in TFIID and Mediator occupancy were observed at all bound promoters following Bdf depletion.
source: We observed modest (~1.7-fold) decreases in TFIID and Mediator occupancy at all bound promoters following Bdf depletion (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: SAGA binding was relatively insensitive to Bdf depletion with only small decreases observed, mostly at CR promoters.
source: In contrast, SAGA binding was relatively insensitive to Bdf depletion with only small decreases observed, mostly at CR promoters.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: Changes measured for different subunits of TFIID or Mediator correlate after Bdf depletion.
source: Importantly, changes measured for different subunits of TFIID or Mediator correlate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Similar results for Bdf-dependent Taf1 binding were observed using the ChIP-seq assay.
source: Using the ChIP-seq assay, similar results were observed for Bdf-dependent Taf1 binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, F and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, F.

claim: Modest binding cooperativity exists between TFIID and Mediator.
source: We confirmed modest binding cooperativity between both factors, but the decreases in TFIID and Mediator binding were significantly stronger after depleting Bdfs (compare Figure 4A, B with C, D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data comparing Med14 and Taf13 depletion effects.

claim: The decreases in TFIID and Mediator binding were significantly stronger after depleting Bdfs compared to depleting Med14 or Taf13.
source: We confirmed modest binding cooperativity between both factors, but the decreases in TFIID and Mediator binding were significantly stronger after depleting Bdfs (compare Figure 4A, B with C, D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparative ChEC-seq data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Bdfs have a role in both TFIID and Mediator recruitment beyond the cooperative interactions of these two factors.
source: This indicates a role of Bdfs in both TFIID and Mediator recruitment beyond the cooperative interactions of these two factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis of factor depletion effects.

claim: Bdfs have independent contributions to the recruitment of TFIID and Mediator.
source: Altogether, our results illustrate that Bdfs have independent contributions to the recruitment of TFIID and Mediator, although, in the absence of Bdfs, both factors are still recruited to promoters at substantial levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChEC-seq data showing partial decreases in factor occupancy.

claim: In the absence of Bdfs, both TFIID and Mediator are still recruited to promoters at substantial levels.
source: Altogether, our results illustrate that Bdfs have independent contributions to the recruitment of TFIID and Mediator, although, in the absence of Bdfs, both factors are still recruited to promoters at substantial levels.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data showing residual factor occupancy after Bdf depletion.

claim: The strong transcription defects upon Bdf depletion are not solely mediated by defects in TFIID and Mediator binding.
source: Our results suggest that the strong transcription defects upon Bdf depletion are not solely mediated by defects in TFIID and Mediator binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the disproportionate transcription defects compared to factor binding defects.

claim: Depletion of either Bdfs or Taf13 caused a global loss of TFIIB, most pronounced at TFIID-dependent promoters.
source: Depletion of either Bdfs or Taf13 caused a global loss of TFIIB, most pronounced at TFIID-dependent promoters (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bdf depletion caused a significantly larger loss of TFIIB at TFIID-dependent promoters than does TFIID depletion.
source: Comparing the defects in TFIIB binding due to Bdf depletion versus TFIID depletion, we found that Bdf depletion caused a significantly larger loss of TFIIB at TFIID-dependent promoters than does TFIID depletion (Figure 5B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparative ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At CR genes, TFIID depletion caused a greater loss in TFIIB signal compared with Bdf depletion.
source: Conversely, at CR genes, we found that TFIID depletion caused a greater loss in TFIIB signal compared with Bdf depletion.
evidence: This is supported by comparative ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Bdfs have a broader role in transcription than solely regulating PIC assembly.
source: However, comparison of transcriptional and TFIIB binding defects caused by Bdf depletion shows that Bdfs have a broader role in transcription than solely regulating PIC assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the disproportionate transcription defects compared to TFIIB binding defects.

claim: At the most Bdf-dependent genes, transcription defects significantly exceed the defect in TFIIB binding.
source: This larger role of Bdfs is especially apparent for the most Bdf-dependent genes where transcription defects significantly exceed the defect in TFIIB binding (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Bdfs have an additional role in transcription that extends beyond organizing a platform for recruitment of PIC components.
source: Combined, our results suggest an additional role of Bdfs in transcription that extend beyond organizing a platform for recruitment of PIC components.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of PIC assembly and transcription data.

claim: At many metazoan promoters, Pol II pauses after transcribing ~20–100 nucleotides.
source: At many metazoan promoters, Pol II pauses after transcribing ~20–100 nucleotides, and release of paused Pol II, mediated by phosphorylation of NELF, DSIF, and the C-terminal repeat domain (CTD) Ser2, is a critical step in gene regulation (Core and Adelman, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Release of paused Pol II is mediated by phosphorylation of NELF, DSIF, and the CTD Ser2.
source: At many metazoan promoters, Pol II pauses after transcribing ~20–100 nucleotides, and release of paused Pol II, mediated by phosphorylation of NELF, DSIF, and the C-terminal repeat domain (CTD) Ser2, is a critical step in gene regulation (Core and Adelman, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Brd4 was shown to be involved in Ser2 phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, Brd4 was shown to be involved in Ser2 phosphorylation (Muhar et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Metazoan-like Pol II pausing does not occur at yeast promoters.
source: While metazoan-like Pol II pausing does not occur at yeast promoters, Pol II stalling and shifts in Pol II distribution under specific conditions have been observed in both budding and fission yeast (Badjatia et al., 2021; Shetty et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pol II stalling and shifts in Pol II distribution under specific conditions have been observed in both budding and fission yeast.
source: While metazoan-like Pol II pausing does not occur at yeast promoters, Pol II stalling and shifts in Pol II distribution under specific conditions have been observed in both budding and fission yeast (Badjatia et al., 2021; Shetty et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The change in transcription following Bdf depletion is not proportional to the loss of Pol II signal, even though the two results show a good correlation.
source: We found that the change in transcription following Bdf depletion is not proportional to the loss of Pol II signal, even though the two results show a good correlation (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The decrease in Pol II signal at the most Bdf-dependent genes is less severe than the loss of transcription.
source: As we observed for TFIIB, the decrease in Pol II signal at the most Bdf-dependent genes is less severe than the loss of transcription.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A similar difference between Pol II signal decrease and transcription loss was not detected after depleting Taf1.
source: Importantly, we did not detect such difference after depleting Taf1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bdf depletion caused a similar loss of Pol II at TSSs of all genes except the first quintile (the least Bdf-dependent genes).
source: Except for the first quintile (the least Bdf-dependent genes), Bdf depletion caused a similar loss of Pol II at TSSs of all genes.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Pol II loss increased further downstream of TSS at the most Bdf-dependent genes until stabilizing at ~400 bp downstream of TSS.
source: Interestingly, the Pol II loss increased further downstream of TSS at the most Bdf-dependent genes until stabilizing at ~400 bp downstream of TSS.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At the least Bdf-dependent genes, the Pol II signal partially recovered in the first ~400 bp downstream of TSS relative to the loss at TSS.
source: Conversely, at the least Bdf-dependent genes, the Pol II signal partially recovered in the first ~400 bp downstream of TSS relative to the loss at TSS.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A decrease of TR was observed at the least Bdf-dependent genes following Bdf depletion.
source: We observed a decrease of TR at the least Bdf-dependent genes and an increase of TR at the most dependent genes following Bdf depletion (Figure 6C and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by traveling ratio analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: An increase of TR was observed at the most Bdf-dependent genes following Bdf depletion.
source: We observed a decrease of TR at the least Bdf-dependent genes and an increase of TR at the most dependent genes following Bdf depletion (Figure 6C and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by traveling ratio analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Analysis of individual genes revealed shifts in Pol II distribution towards 3′ or 5′ ends of genes after Bdf depletion.
source: Analysis of individual genes revealed shifts in Pol II distribution towards 3′ or 5′ ends of genes, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Similar changes in Pol II distribution were not detected after depleting Taf1.
source: We did not detect similar changes in Pol II distribution after depleting Taf1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The change in TR after depleting Bdfs correlates with the change in transcription at individual genes.
source: Importantly, the change in TR after depleting Bdfs correlates with the change in transcription at individual genes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There is a modest correlation between the change in TR and the loss of TFIIB at promoters.
source: There is also a modest correlation between the change in TR and the loss of TFIIB at promoters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: At least a subset of the most Bdf-dependent genes experience transcription defects both at the initiation and elongation stages upon Bdf depletion.
source: Combined with our earlier findings, this suggests that at least a subset of the most Bdf-dependent genes experience transcription defects both at the initiation and elongation stages upon Bdf depletion.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of initiation and elongation data.

claim: The combined initiation and elongation defects explain the disproportionally large decrease in the amount of nascent RNA at the most Bdf-dependent genes.
source: This explains the disproportionally large decrease in the amount of nascent RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of initiation and elongation defects.

claim: More efficient elongation at the least Bdf-dependent genes partially nullifies the initiation defects, leading to little total change in transcription upon Bdf depletion.
source: On the other hand, more efficient elongation at the least Bdf-dependent genes seems to partially nullify the initiation defects, leading to little total change in transcription upon Bdf depletion (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of initiation and elongation data.

claim: At the most Bdf-dependent genes, Pol II becomes hypophosphorylated on Ser2 and, to a lesser extent, on Ser5 after depleting Bdfs.
source: In agreement with the above findings that the most Bdf-dependent genes have a defect in elongation, Pol II becomes hypophosphorylated on Ser2 and, to a lesser extent, on Ser5 after depleting Bdfs.
evidence: This is supported by CTD phosphorylation analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: At the least Bdf-dependent genes, Pol II becomes weakly hyperphosphorylated after depleting Bdfs.
source: Conversely, at the least Bdf-dependent genes, Pol II becomes weakly hyperphosphorylated, in agreement with the suggestion that elongation becomes more efficient at this gene set upon Bdf depletion.
evidence: This is supported by CTD phosphorylation analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Similar changes in Pol II phosphorylation were not observed after Taf1 depletion.
source: Importantly, we did not observe similar changes in Pol II phosphorylation after Taf1 depletion, which validates that Bdfs have a TFIID-independent role in regulating transcriptional elongation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by CTD phosphorylation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Bdfs have a TFIID-independent role in regulating transcriptional elongation.
source: Importantly, we did not observe similar changes in Pol II phosphorylation after Taf1 depletion, which validates that Bdfs have a TFIID-independent role in regulating transcriptional elongation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Bdf versus Taf1 depletion on Pol II phosphorylation.

claim: Bur1 and Ctk1 are homologues of metazoan Cdk9 and Cdk12/13.
source: Bur1 and Ctk1, homologues of metazoan Cdk9 and Cdk12/13, are responsible for CTD Ser2P marks in yeast.
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinase homology.

claim: Bur1 and Ctk1 are responsible for CTD Ser2P marks in yeast.
source: Bur1 and Ctk1, homologues of metazoan Cdk9 and Cdk12/13, are responsible for CTD Ser2P marks in yeast.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast CTD kinases.

claim: The relative gene body occupancies of Bur1 and Ctk1, but not of Spt5, correlate with gene dependence on Bdfs.
source: Interestingly, the relative gene body occupancies of Bur1 and Ctk1, but not of Spt5, correlate with gene dependence on Bdfs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Approximately twofold increases in occupancy of both Bur1 and Ctk1 relative to Rpb1 were observed at the least Bdf-dependent genes after Bdf depletion.
source: We observed approximately twofold increases in occupancy of both kinases relative to Rpb1 at the least Bdf-dependent genes, a result that agrees with observed CTD hyperphosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: At the rest of the genes, the relative occupancy of both Bur1 and Ctk1 further increased after Bdf depletion, correlating with gene dependence on Bdfs.
source: Surprisingly, at the rest of the genes, the relative occupancy of both kinases further increased, correlating with gene dependence on Bdfs.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: A uniform, small (~1.4-fold) increase in Spt5 occupancy, normalized to Rpb1, was observed at all tested genes after Bdf depletion.
source: In contrast, we observed a uniform, small (~1.4-fold) increase in Spt5 occupancy, normalized to Rpb1, at all tested genes (Figure 6F and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Bur1 and Ctk1 accumulate at the 5′ end of the most Bdf-dependent genes until stabilizing at ~400 bp downstream of TSS after Bdf depletion.
source: Similarly as for Rpb1, but showing the opposite trend, Bur1 and Ctk1 accumulate at the 5′ end of the most Bdf-dependent genes until stabilizing at ~400 bp downstream of TSS.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Changes in the recruitment of Spt5 and CTD kinases cannot account for the function of Bdfs in transcription elongation.
source: These results illustrate that changes in the recruitment of Spt5 and CTD kinases cannot account for the function of Bdfs in transcription elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the paradoxical increase in kinase occupancy despite decreased CTD phosphorylation.

claim: The observed defect in elongation is restricted to the first ~400 bp in the transcribed region.
source: They also provide further evidence that the observed defect in elongation is restricted to the first ~400 bp in the transcribed region.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial pattern of Pol II and kinase changes.

claim: Bdf functions extend beyond solely regulating TFIID as expression from most genes is more sensitive to Bdf versus TFIID depletion.
source: We explored transcription dependence on Bdf1/2, their genome-wide binding patterns, and their interplay with key components of the transcriptional machinery. We found that Bdf functions extend beyond solely regulating TFIID as expression from most genes is more sensitive to Bdf versus TFIID depletion.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by comparative RNA-seq data.

claim: The roles of yeast BET factors are surprisingly similar to their human equivalents.
source: Our work reveals that the roles of yeast BET factors are surprisingly similar to their human equivalents and suggests conserved mechanisms of BET function across eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by comparative analysis of yeast and human data.

claim: The organization and amino acid sequence of Bdf1 is more similar to human BET factors than to the hTaf1 BDs.
source: However, we found that that the organization and amino acid sequence of Bdf1 is more similar to human BET factors than to the hTaf1 BDs.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and sequence analysis.

claim: Bdfs regulate a similar set of genes as TFIID, but there are important differences.
source: Our results showed that Bdfs regulate a similar set of genes as TFIID, but that there are important differences.
evidence: This is supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Transcription from most genes defined as CR is largely insensitive to Bdf depletion.
source: Transcription from most genes defined earlier as CR is largely insensitive to Bdf depletion, while a large subset of TFIID-dependent genes is significantly more affected by Bdf versus TFIID depletion.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: A large subset of TFIID-dependent genes is significantly more affected by Bdf versus TFIID depletion.
source: Transcription from most genes defined earlier as CR is largely insensitive to Bdf depletion, while a large subset of TFIID-dependent genes is significantly more affected by Bdf versus TFIID depletion.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Bdf1/2 are found together with TFIID at many promoters and contribute to TFIID recruitment.
source: Genome-wide mapping revealed that Bdf1/2 are found together with TFIID at many promoters and that they contribute to TFIID recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data.

claim: A substantial fraction of TFIID is still bound to promoters in the absence of Bdfs.
source: However, a substantial fraction of TFIID is still bound to promoters in the absence of Bdfs, in agreement with the sub-stoichiometric association between Bdf1 and TFIID (Sanders et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data and citation to prior literature.

claim: Human BET proteins were shown to associate with TFIID in a proteomic screen.
source: Interestingly, human BET proteins were shown to associate with TFIID in a proteomic screen and both Brd4 and hTaf1 were proposed to have synergistic effects on gene expression and cell growth (Lambert et al., 2019; Sdelci et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both Brd4 and hTaf1 were proposed to have synergistic effects on gene expression and cell growth.
source: Interestingly, human BET proteins were shown to associate with TFIID in a proteomic screen and both Brd4 and hTaf1 were proposed to have synergistic effects on gene expression and cell growth (Lambert et al., 2019; Sdelci et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: hTaf1 BDs have the same substrate specificity as BET BDs.
source: Finally, hTaf1 BDs have the same substrate specificity as BET BDs and both Brd4 and TFIID are bound to the majority of active promoters in human cells (Bhagwat et al., 2016; Lauberth et al., 2013; Slaughter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both Brd4 and TFIID are bound to the majority of active promoters in human cells.
source: Finally, hTaf1 BDs have the same substrate specificity as BET BDs and both Brd4 and TFIID are bound to the majority of active promoters in human cells (Bhagwat et al., 2016; Lauberth et al., 2013; Slaughter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cooperation between BET factors and TFIID is a conserved feature of eukaryotic gene regulation.
source: Based on our findings and the presented evidence from human cells, we propose that cooperation between BET factors and TFIID is a conserved feature of eukaryotic gene regulation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined evidence from yeast and human studies.

claim: The gain of BDs by metazoan TFIID may result from the increased complexity of gene expression programs and allow for BET-independent TFIID interactions with acetylated histone H4.
source: The gain of BDs by metazoan TFIID may result from the increased complexity of gene expression programs and allow for BET-independent TFIID interactions with acetylated histone H4.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary adaptation.

claim: Brd4 interacts with Mediator and participates in Mediator recruitment to enhancers and promoters.
source: Brd4 interacts with Mediator and participates in Mediator recruitment to enhancers and promoters (Bhagwat et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bdfs are important for normal levels of Mediator occupancy.
source: Our experiments revealed that Bdfs are important for normal levels of Mediator occupancy.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data.

claim: Mediator was proposed to be recruited cooperatively with TFIID.
source: Mediator was proposed to be recruited cooperatively with TFIID (Grünberg et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2002; Knoll et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The contribution of Bdfs to Mediator recruitment surpasses that of TFIID.
source: We confirmed this modest cooperativity, but we found that the contribution of Bdfs to Mediator recruitment surpasses that of TFIID.
evidence: This is supported by comparative ChEC-seq data.

claim: TFIID and Mediator act as molecular scaffolds to organize the recruitment of other components of transcriptional machinery.
source: There is strong evidence that TFIID and Mediator act as molecular scaffolds to organize the recruitment of other components of transcriptional machinery (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Patel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human Mediator and Brd4 participate in the formation of dynamic nuclear condensates at the sites of active transcription.
source: Human Mediator and Brd4 were also found to participate in the formation of dynamic nuclear condensates at the sites of active transcription (Han et al., 2020; Sabari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A recent study suggested cooperation of yeast TFIID and Mediator in restricting the diffusion of PIC components to shared subnuclear territories to facilitate gene transcription.
source: Finally, a recent study suggested cooperation of yeast TFIID and Mediator in restricting the diffusion of PIC components to shared subnuclear territories in order to facilitate gene transcription (Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Chromatin tethered yeast BET factors serve as a nucleation center for dynamic recruitment of Mediator and TFIID, which in turn create a platform for efficient PIC assembly.
source: We propose that chromatin tethered yeast BET factors serve as a nucleation center for dynamic recruitment of Mediator and TFIID, which in turn create a platform for efficient PIC assembly.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The role of Bdf1/2 in organizing PIC assembly is widespread and likely complementary to the action of sequence-specific TFs.
source: This role of Bdf1/2 seems widespread and likely complementary to the action of sequence-specific TFs (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: At the least Bdf-dependent genes, a modest decrease in TFIID, Mediator, and TFIIB recruitment after Bdf depletion did not translate into appreciable defects in mRNA synthesis.
source: At the least Bdf-dependent genes, we observed a modest decrease in TFIID, Mediator, and TFIIB recruitment after Bdf depletion, which did not translate into appreciable defects in mRNA synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by combined analysis of ChEC-seq, ChIP-seq, and RNA-seq data.

claim: At the most Bdf-dependent genes, the loss of transcription exceeded the loss of Mediator, TFIID, TFIIB, and Pol II recruitment.
source: Conversely, at the most Bdf-dependent genes, the loss of transcription exceeded the loss of Mediator, TFIID, TFIIB, and Pol II recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by combined analysis of ChEC-seq, ChIP-seq, and RNA-seq data.

claim: At CR genes and at a small subset of TFIID-dependent genes, Bdf depletion results in a 3′ shift in Pol II distribution and increased CTD Ser2 phosphorylation.
source: At CR genes and at a small subset of TFIID-dependent genes, Bdf depletion results in a 3′ shift in Pol II distribution and increased CTD Ser2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by Pol II ChIP-seq and CTD phosphorylation data.

claim: The 3′ shift in Pol II distribution and increased CTD Ser2 phosphorylation at CR genes suggests more efficient early elongation in the absence of Bdfs.
source: This suggests more efficient early elongation of these genes in the absence of Bdfs.
evidence: This is inferred from the Pol II distribution and phosphorylation changes.

claim: Bdf depletion at many TFIID-dependent genes causes Pol II accumulation at 5′ gene ends and a loss of CTD Ser2 phosphorylation.
source: In contrast, Bdf depletion at many TFIID-dependent genes causes Pol II accumulation at 5′ gene ends and a loss of CTD Ser2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by Pol II ChIP-seq and CTD phosphorylation data.

claim: The change in Pol II profile after Bdf depletion at TFIID-dependent genes is similar to the defects in pause release caused by BET depletion in human cells.
source: This change in Pol II profile is similar to the defects in pause release caused by BET depletion in human cells (Muhar et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited prior literature.

claim: At yeast genes, the combined initiation and elongation defects resulting from Bdf depletion lead to a large decrease in mRNA synthesis.
source: At these yeast genes, the combined initiation and elongation defects resulting from Bdf depletion lead to a large decrease in mRNA synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of initiation and elongation data.

claim: Acute stress in Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells causes Pol II stalling at the +2 nucleosome, which overlaps with the region where dominant changes in Pol II distribution are observed after Bdf depletion.
source: Interestingly, it was recently shown that acute stress in Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells causes Pol II stalling at the +2 nucleosome, which overlaps with the region where we observe dominant changes in Pol II distribution (Badjatia et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CTD Ser2 residues in yeast are phosphorylated by kinases Bur1 and Ctk1.
source: CTD Ser2 residues in yeast are phosphorylated by kinases Bur1 and Ctk1, homologues of metazoan Cdk9 and Cdk12/13, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast CTD kinases.

claim: Ctk1 is the dominant CTD kinase in yeast.
source: Ctk1 is the dominant CTD kinase in yeast while in metazoans Cdk12/13 seems to be less important, although the interplay between Cdk9 and Cdk12/13 is poorly understood (Harlen and Churchman, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In metazoans Cdk12/13 seems to be less important than Cdk9, although the interplay between Cdk9 and Cdk12/13 is poorly understood.
source: Ctk1 is the dominant CTD kinase in yeast while in metazoans Cdk12/13 seems to be less important, although the interplay between Cdk9 and Cdk12/13 is poorly understood (Harlen and Churchman, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: At Bdf-independent genes, depletion of Bdfs results in a modest increase of Bur1 and Ctk1 occupancy normalized to Rpb1 level, which agrees with a gain of CTD Ser2P marks at these genes.
source: At Bdf-independent genes, depletion of Bdfs results in a modest increase of Bur1 and Ctk1 occupancy normalized to Rpb1 level, and this agrees with a gain of CTD Ser2P marks at these genes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: At Bdf-dependent genes, the occupancy of both Bur1 and Ctk1 relative to Rpb1 increased significantly in the first ~400 bp of transcribed region after Bdf depletion, even though CTD Ser2 phosphorylation decreases.
source: Surprisingly, at Bdf-dependent genes, the occupancy of both kinases relative to Rpb1 increased significantly in the first ~400 bp of transcribed region after Bdf depletion, even though CTD Ser2 phosphorylation decreases.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Depletion of Brd4 or all BET factors in human cells results in a small increase in Cdk9 and Cyclin T1 chromatin occupancy, even though it causes a decrease in CTD Ser2P marks and a defect in pause release.
source: Interestingly, depletion of Brd4 or all BET factors in human cells was shown to result in a small increase in Cdk9 and Cyclin T1 chromatin occupancy, even though it causes a decrease in CTD Ser2P marks and a defect in pause release (Muhar et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is not known if Brd4 affects Cdk12/13 recruitment.
source: It is not known if Brd4 affects Cdk12/13 recruitment.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Brd4 was shown to release Hexim1-mediated inhibition of Cdk9 in vitro, thus acting as a positive regulator of P-TEFb.
source: Brd4 was shown to release Hexim1-mediated inhibition of Cdk9 in vitro, thus acting as a positive regulator of P-TEFb (Itzen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: It was proposed that Brd2 and Brd4 have kinase activity and that Brd4 is directly connected to CTD Ser2 phosphorylation independently of P-TEFb.
source: It was also proposed that Brd2 and Brd4 have kinase activity and that Brd4 is directly connected to CTD Ser2 phosphorylation independently of P-TEFb (Denis and Green, 1996; Devaiah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bdf1 was proposed to have an intrinsic kinase activity.
source: Bdf1 was also proposed to have an intrinsic kinase activity, which raises an intriguing prospect of its direct involvement in CTD phosphorylation that, if correct, would provide an explanation for our results (Matangkasombut et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CTD hypophosphorylation at BET-dependent genes may result from defects in recruitment and/or reduction in function of other elongation factors.
source: Finally, it is possible that CTD hypophosphorylation at BET-dependent genes may result from defects in recruitment and/or reduction in function of other elongation factors.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The role(s) of the BET factors in elongation are unresolved in both yeast and metazoan systems.
source: Since the role(s) of the BET factors in elongation are unresolved in both systems, it will be of great interest to determine whether the yeast and metazoan factors use similar mechanisms to regulate elongation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Redundancy between three (Brd2, Brd3, Brd4) of the four mammalian BET factors was proposed based on their ubiquitous expression in most tissues, similar binding patterns, and because they are all essential for embryonic development.
source: Redundancy between three (Brd2, Brd3, Brd4) of the four mammalian BET factors was proposed based on their ubiquitous expression in most tissues, similar binding patterns, and because they are all essential for embryonic development (Gyuris et al., 2009; Khoueiry et al., 2019; Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The extent of redundancy between mammalian BET factors is poorly understood.
source: The extent of this redundancy is poorly understood because only a few context-specific examples of shared functions of BET factors have been reported (Gilan et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2011; Stonestrom et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In most studies, the roles of BET factors in transcriptional regulation were attributed to Brd4 alone.
source: In most studies, the roles of BET factors in transcriptional regulation were attributed to Brd4 alone (Muhar et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2021; Zuber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Yeast BET proteins are functionally redundant under normal growth conditions, with Bdf1 being the dominant factor.
source: Our data indicate that yeast BET proteins are functionally redundant under normal growth conditions, with Bdf1 being the dominant factor.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from this study.

claim: The changes in transcription following depletion of Bdf1 or Bdf1/2 are highly correlated.
source: The changes in transcription following depletion of Bdf1 or Bdf1/2 are highly correlated, while depletion of Bdf2 does not have significant consequences for the cell.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Depletion of Bdf2 does not have significant consequences for the cell.
source: The changes in transcription following depletion of Bdf1 or Bdf1/2 are highly correlated, while depletion of Bdf2 does not have significant consequences for the cell.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Bdf1 and Bdf2 have nearly identical genome-wide binding patterns.
source: In addition, Bdf1 and Bdf2 have nearly identical genome-wide binding patterns and Bdf2 redistributes from CR to TFIID-dependent genes upon Bdf1 depletion.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data analysis.

claim: Bdf2 redistributes from CR to TFIID-dependent genes upon Bdf1 depletion.
source: In addition, Bdf1 and Bdf2 have nearly identical genome-wide binding patterns and Bdf2 redistributes from CR to TFIID-dependent genes upon Bdf1 depletion.
evidence: This is supported by ChEC-seq data analysis.

claim: Bdf2 overexpression can suppress temperature- and salt-sensitive phenotypes in a bdf1 deletion strain.
source: Interestingly, it was reported that Bdf2 overexpression can suppress temperature- and salt-sensitive phenotypes in a bdf1 deletion strain, but, at the same time, Bdf1 was found to be a negative regulator of Bdf2 expression (Fu et al., 2013; Matangkasombut et al., 2000).

claim: Bdf1 was found to be a negative regulator of Bdf2 expression.
source: Interestingly, it was reported that Bdf2 overexpression can suppress temperature- and salt-sensitive phenotypes in a bdf1 deletion strain, but, at the same time, Bdf1 was found to be a negative regulator of Bdf2 expression (Fu et al., 2013; Matangkasombut et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Approximately two-fold upregulation of BDF2 transcription was observed following Bdf1 depletion.
source: This latter finding is also supported by our RNA-seq results where we observed approximately two-fold upregulation of BDF2 transcription following Bdf1 depletion.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data from this study.

claim: A similar interplay between human BET factors in regulating expression of other family members was recently proposed.
source: Importantly, a similar interplay between human BET factors in regulating expression of other family members was recently proposed (Lambert et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Many of the most BET-sensitive genes in both yeast and human systems lack a TATA element in their promoters.
source: Many of the most BET-sensitive genes in both systems lack a TATA element in their promoters and control highly similar cellular processes.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of yeast and human data.

claim: The most BET-sensitive genes in both yeast and human systems control highly similar cellular processes.
source: Many of the most BET-sensitive genes in both systems lack a TATA element in their promoters and control highly similar cellular processes.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis.

claim: BET proteins are universally involved in the recruitment of Mediator to chromatin.
source: BET proteins are also universally involved in the recruitment of Mediator to chromatin and modulation of transcriptional elongation.
evidence: This is supported by data from both yeast and human studies.

claim: BET proteins are universally involved in modulation of transcriptional elongation.
source: BET proteins are also universally involved in the recruitment of Mediator to chromatin and modulation of transcriptional elongation.
evidence: This is supported by data from both yeast and human studies.

claim: The yeast model system offers unique opportunities for a detailed investigation of different aspects of BET biology.
source: Considering the relative simplicity compared to metazoans, the yeast model system offers unique opportunities for a detailed investigation of different aspects of BET biology, and this work provides a foundation for these future studies.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the value of the yeast system.
